entities.summary:
Bai Renfu (c. 1226–1306), also known by his courtesy name Bai Pu, was a preeminent Chinese playwright and poet of the Yuan dynasty, a period when the Mongol-led empire fostered a vibrant theatrical tradition. Born into a scholarly family in Shanxi during the tumultuous transition from the Jin to the Yuan, his literary career flourished in Dadu (modern Beijing) and Hangzhou. He is recognized as one of the "Four Great Yuan Playwrights," alongside Guan Hanqing, Ma Zhiyuan, and Zheng Guangzu, whose collective genius defined the Golden Age of *zaju* drama, a form of Chinese opera combining poetry, music, song, and acrobatics. His works offered sophisticated narratives and lyrical verse that deeply resonated with both common audiences and the literati, solidifying *zaju*'s place as a dominant cultural force.

Bai Renfu's most celebrated work is *Wutong Yu* (Rain on the Parasol Trees), a four-act *zaju* play with a prologue that dramatizes the tragic love story between Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty and his concubine Yang Guifei amidst the An Lushan Rebellion (755-763 CE). Through poignant arias and vivid characterizations, Bai Renfu explored themes of imperial devotion, political intrigue, and the ephemeral nature of glory, particularly focusing on the emperor's grief following Yang Guifei's forced suicide. He composed at least 15 other *zaju* plays, though only three survive complete, including *Qiangtou Mashang* (Over the Wall on Horseback) and *Dongqiang Jishi* (The Story of the Eastern Wall), which explore romantic themes and social conventions. His poetic contributions also include *sanquetu* (loose verse) and song lyrics, showcasing his versatility and mastery of literary forms.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bai Renfu was a pivotal figure in the Golden Age of Yuan drama, with his masterpiece *Wutong Yu* becoming a canonical work that influenced subsequent Chinese opera forms like Kunqu and Peking opera. His contributions helped define a major genre and era in Chinese cultural history.
